So, of all the jargon in that list....

Linux: This is what's called the kernel. It's the core of the operating system, originally developed by linus torvalds back in the 90s because GNU was taking too long.

Mint: This is the particular distro. Mint are a group who package linux with installers and useful programs so regular people can use it, rather than having to configure everything themselves.

Rosa: This is the release version, it's just their naming convention for each different release (I think they use women's names). Petra, Quercos, Rosa etc. In a few months there'll be an update and it'll be Linux: Mint S-something.

Cinnamon: Now we're getting into an area where you have some choice. Cinnamon is a desktop, also developed by the mint group. If you search cinnamon desktop on youtube you should see a few examples and work out if it's right for you.

XFCE: Another desktop, developed by another group. It's focused on being small and fast, so it runs well on old hardware and runs amazingly on new hardware. It's not very fancy (looks and feels a bit like windowsXP) but if you play alot of games or do graphics intensive work of some kind then this would be a good choice. Also, anyone who knows their way around windows will know what they're doing.

KDE: A desktop developed by another release group (you can get Linux: KDE). Mint include their desktop as an option. It's quite popular, but a bit different to windows. See youtube to check it out.

I've been using Linux for more than 10 years and I still don't know all of the answers. These responses don't help a ton either.

So, as it's been stated before, these are all desktop environments (DE's)... but let's take a stab at explaining why they are different to help this make things more clear.

First, let's compare one version of Windows with another version of Windows... let's just say XP with Win7, for the hell of it, although it doesn't really matter, since they're all essentially the same:

In XP, you're started with a blue taskbar and an oval green Start Menu button with the Windows logo and the word "START" on it... you can change the theme here to make XP look more like 95/98, but that's about it. But Win7 gives you a transparent taskbar with a round blue Start Menu button with only the Windows logo, where the only real things you can theme are the colors and level of transparency... you can't theme it to look like XP or 95/98. The icons are different, the window boarders are different, and the window animations (when you minimize, restore, and maximize a window) are different.

But, for the most part, the underlying code is the same. They're still based on a Fat/NTFS file system, they're both running Command Prompt, and they're both executing the same code... when you download an application, you download either a 64-bit or 32-bit EXE, not an XP or Win7 EXE, right?

These differences can be found using any two versions of Windows, as they're all running the same base code (with a few enhancements from generation to generation) but they all look and behave differently.

These differences are with the graphical user interface (GUI) and NOT in the underlying code (for the most part). This would essentially be the difference between one DE and another. Each version of Linux is running the same (for the most part) kernel, but looks and behaves (on a GUI level) differently from one another, depending on what DE is installed.

Now, let's compare Windows with OSX. This will be messy, as it's not an apples-to-apples comparison, but let's just try it anyway:

Each has different base applications...

Windows OSX
Notepad TextEdit
Command Prompt Terminal
Internet Explorer Safari
Windows Media Quicktime

And the list goes on and on, but these are just a couple of examples of what's different between the two.

When you open a window (Notepad, browser, etc.) that window has a specific boarder. In Win, the buttons to control that window (min, max, close) are in the top right... but in OSX they're on the top left (close, min, max). The boarders are also stylized differently, and behave differently when you interact with them... You can snap them to a side of the screen, snap them to the left/right half of your monitor, or whatever the OPERATING SYSTEM (this is an important term we'll come back to later) allows you to do.

In Win, you only have one desktop where you do all of your work. In OSX, you can "shuffle" through multiple "workspaces." You also have an Expose function to "manage" multiple windows and desktop workspaces.

The icons between the two are different, as are the style of cursors.

Essentially, there are too many differences between the two to list like this... If each OS had the same underlying code, these differences would be attributed to the DE as the functional code is the same, but the graphical user interface (GUI) is different and acts differently.

Now, let's consider Linux. The kernels for each Linux distribution (distro) are essentially the same, but the DE and package manager between them are different. So, since you're talking about different versions of Linux Mint, each has the same package manager and the same underlying functional code, but a different DE. In other words, each version of Mint will function the same, but look and behave (on a GUI level) differently.

This is because Linux is a kernel and not an OS (told you we'd come back to this). The kernel is a bare-bones piece of code that makes your computer work, but isn't what makes your computer usable. I don't want to get too detailed, so we'll use another example: Imagine booting into the command line only... you don't know what to do with that, and it's not very helpful to you right now (although it will be)... that would be like having just a kernel... whereas having an OS will give you a GUI with a login manager and icons and a Start menu you can click on and manipulate. This is where your DE adds a GUI and all of the programs (a browser, Notepad, your office suite, etc) become functional in.

But not all DE's are created the same:

Some DE's offer more of what I like to call "flair" where you have animations, transparencies, and other "neat things" that don't add to the functionality, but add visual appeal. Naturally, all of this flair will require more system resources than a DE that has no flair (think Vista with all of its flair vs XP with generally no flair). What you're going to have to do is find a "sweet spot" for you and your hardware... a DE that is visual appealing to you, but also bare-bones enough so that your hardware can handle it without lagging.

And this is why there are so many versions of Mint... or any other distro, TBH.

The best advice I can give you here is to just download different versions and use them. Find one that you like, and start there. That, or watch YouTube videos of Mint running the different DE's, and find one that you like.

Now that I've typed all of this out, and you've read it, here's the best/worst part: NONE OF IT MATTERS.

Just listen to me for a second... Yes, you're new and trying to feel your way around Linux. That's great. But once you get used to it, you'll learn how to install and remove DE's through a simple line of text, and you'll be able to change things to however you like. Don't let your Windows/Mac experiences carry over... you can change anything on a Linux box, whenever you want, as long as you have either the know-how or good help (which I'm/we're here to provide).

Remember how I said the kernel was the functional code and the DE was the GUI? Well, that means you can swap out the GUI/DE for another GUI/DE and end up with the same functional code, meaning that your system will work the same way, just look/behave a little differently.
